text:
Statistics is the round most data science candidates are rustiest on. The formulas come back quickly. What gives people away is a single sentence: a p-value read as the chance the null is true, or a ninety-five percent interval read as a ninety-five percent chance. Nineteen questions follow, in the order the ideas build: sampling, then estimation, then testing. Sixteen come with a figure. The last three are short. Everything here crosses one bridge, from a sample to its population. Start at the two ends.

Question one. What's the difference between a parameter and a statistic? A parameter describes the population, like its true mean, and it's usually unknown. This population is simulated, so we can see it: five point oh two. A statistic is computed from a sample, like the mean of these fifty values, five point five seven. It estimates the parameter. Question two. What is the standard error, or S E, and how does it differ from the standard deviation? The standard deviation is the spread of single values: about five here. The standard error is the spread of a statistic, like the mean, from one sample to the next. For independent draws, it's the standard deviation over the square root of n: about point seven, for samples of fifty. Four times the data halves it: point three six at two hundred. The standard deviation needn't shrink at all. Question three. What is a sampling distribution? The distribution of a statistic across every possible sample of the same size. Draw two thousand samples of fifty, and drop each mean as a dot. The data was lopsided, but the means pile up into a narrow bell around five. Its spread is the standard error: point seven oh by simulation, point seven one by the formula.
